paras.text: Contracts, HIFA, Risk and Warranty, Audio Lecture

This chapter is about seven questions out of your fifty business and law questions, and it is the most trap heavy territory on the whole exam. Not because the law is hard. Because Michigan has four different statutes here that each do a completely different job, and almost every wrong answer on this part of the test is built by taking one statute's rule and hanging it on a different statute's name.
So the goal of this chapter is not memorizing. It is separation. If you can keep these four laws in four separate boxes, the traps stop working on you.
Idea one. The map. Four laws, four jobs.

Law one is M C L five seventy point eleven fourteen, inside the Construction Lien Act. Its job is your lien. It says a contractor has no construction lien on a residential structure unless the work was done under a written contract, and any amendments or additions to that contract are also in writing. The contract must contain a statement that residential builders, electricians, plumbers, and mechanical contractors are required to be licensed, and if your work requires a license, it must say you are licensed and include your license number. There is no dollar threshold. A five hundred dollar handyman job and a two hundred thousand dollar addition are treated exactly alike. And a verbal change order means the added scope carries no lien protection.

Law two is M C L three thirty nine point twenty four twelve, in the Occupational Code. Its job is the courthouse door. An unlicensed builder cannot sue to collect compensation for residential work. You can do the work. You just cannot use the courts to get paid for it.

Law three is M C L three thirty nine point twenty four oh three. Its job is licensure, and this is where the famous six hundred dollar number lives. Work where labor and materials combined come to under six hundred dollars is exempt from the licensure requirement.

Hear that clearly, because it is the single most swapped fact in this chapter. Six hundred dollars is a licensure exemption and nothing else. It is not a written contract trigger. If an answer choice tells you that contracts over six hundred dollars must be in writing under HIFA, that answer is wrong twice, wrong about the number's job and wrong about which statute it lives in.

Law four is HIFA, the Home Improvement Finance Act, Act three thirty two of nineteen sixty five, M C L four forty five point eleven oh one and following. Its job is financing. Not contracts generally. Financing.
Question. Which of those four laws decides whether your contract has to be in writing to protect your lien, and which one owns the six hundred dollar number. Say it out loud.

Five seventy point eleven fourteen, the lien act, owns the written contract rule, at any dollar amount. Three thirty nine point twenty four oh three owns the six hundred dollars, and it is only about needing a license.
Idea two. When HIFA actually applies, which is narrower than people think.

HIFA applies only when the homeowner is paying on credit through you. An installment contract or a charge agreement with the contractor. And only when the cash price is more than three hundred dollars. Exactly three hundred does not count, it has to exceed three hundred.

Now the exclusions, because they are the easier way to spot a HIFA question. New home construction is completely excluded. Commercial property is excluded. A loan the homeowner gets directly from their own bank is excluded, because then you are not the one extending the credit. And free standing appliances, a stove or a refrigerator, are excluded.
So the picture is this. Existing home, improvement work, and you are carrying the paper. That is HIFA. Cash, or the homeowner's own bank loan, and HIFA never enters the room.
And one trap to bury. There is no section four forty five point eleven oh eight. It does not exist. Any answer built on it is invented.

Question. You are financing a twelve thousand dollar roof for a homeowner on an installment contract, on a house they have lived in for ten years. HIFA, yes or no. Then change one fact, the homeowner takes a loan from their credit union and pays you in full. HIFA now.
Yes to the first, you are extending the credit on an existing home above three hundred dollars. No to the second, their own bank loan is excluded.
Idea three. What HIFA makes you put on the paper.
When HIFA applies, it is fussy, and the exam tests the fussiness.

The contract must be dated and in writing, with the printed portion in at least eight point type. The words home improvement installment contract must appear in at least ten point bold, either at the top or directly above the buyer's signature. Eight point body, ten point bold heading.

There is a required notice to the buyer in bold type carrying four messages. Do not sign before you read it. You are entitled to a completely filled in copy. You may pay off early and get a partial refund of the finance charge. And you may rescind the contract.

The money has to be itemized, not lumped. Cash price. Down payment. Unpaid cash balance. Insurance premiums if any. Official fees. Principal amount financed. The finance charge stated in dollars. The time balance, the number and amount of the installments, and the time sale price.

And if one installment is a balloon, meaning substantially bigger than the others, the contract needs a bold legend saying this contract is not payable in installments of equal amounts, with that amount and its due date spelled out.

Then the rule that is worth a question all by itself. You must hand the buyer a completed copy of the contract at the time it is signed. Until that completed copy is delivered, the buyer is not obligated to pay you anything. That is section twelve oh four. Not a technicality, a suspension of their duty to pay.
Idea four. The two rescission clocks, which is the biggest trap in the chapter.
Slow down here, because these two get swapped constantly.
Under HIFA, the buyer may rescind until five P M on the business day following the date of the contract. One business day, ending at five in the afternoon.

That is not the three day right you have heard about your whole career. The three day right lives in a different statute entirely, the Home Solicitation Sales Act, and it runs to midnight of the third business day.

Say both, and attach each one to its statute. HIFA, five P M, next business day, because it is about financing. Home solicitation, midnight, third business day, because it is about being sold to in your own kitchen.

And here is the part that separates the people who understand it from the people who memorized it. If a question describes a door to door sale with contractor financing, the buyer gets both rights. They are different statutes doing different jobs, so they stack.
Question. Storm chaser signs a homeowner at the kitchen table on Monday, with financing through the contractor. What cancellation rights does that homeowner have.

Both. The HIFA right until five P M on the next business day, and the home solicitation right until midnight of the third business day. Whichever is more generous is not the point, the buyer holds both.
Idea five. What HIFA forbids you from putting in the contract.
Section twelve oh six bans a list of provisions outright.

You cannot make the buyer waive claims or defenses, either against you or against a finance company that buys the paper from you. You cannot give the holder power to accelerate the balance arbitrarily when the buyer is not in default. You cannot make the buyer waive the right to sue over illegal collection tactics. You cannot authorize breaking into the property or breaching the peace to repossess.

And here is the one builders get wrong, because it contradicts what is true everywhere else. You cannot put a liquidated damages clause in a HIFA contract that pays you for the buyer's cancellation or rescission.

Understand the contrast, because the exam will test the contrast. In an ordinary construction contract a reasonable liquidated damages clause is enforceable, per day delay damages for example, as long as it is a genuine pre estimate of the harm and not a penalty. In a HIFA installment contract, liquidated damages for cancellation are flatly prohibited. The offending clause is void, though the rest of the contract survives.

On top of all that, section fourteen oh nine says no act, agreement, or statement of the buyer is a valid waiver of any protection under the act. The buyer cannot sign away HIFA rights even if they want to. So there is no clever clause that gets you out of this.

Willfully violating HIFA is a misdemeanor. Up to ninety days in jail, a fine up to five hundred dollars, or both, for a first offense. Repeat offenses go up to a year. And paying somebody a reward or a referral fee to procure a home improvement finance contract is prohibited too.
Idea six. The Home Solicitation Sales Act, and the emergency waiver that matters in your real business.

The Home Solicitation Sales Act is Act two twenty seven of nineteen seventy one, M C L four forty five point one eleven through one seventeen. It applies to seller solicited sales at the buyer's home. The classic picture is the storm chaser at the kitchen table.

The buyer can cancel until midnight of the third business day after signing. And note how cancellation counts. A mailed cancellation is effective when it is dropped in the mailbox, properly addressed with postage paid. Not when you receive it. So a cancellation can be effective days before you know it happened.

The contract must carry the cancellation statement right next to the signature line, plus a notice of cancellation form in duplicate. And you cannot send a courier to collect the buyer's payment at the house before the three days run out.
Now the emergency exception, and this one you should learn for work, not just for the exam. To cut off the buyer's cancellation right in an emergency, three things must all be true.

One, the buyer asked for the goods or services without delay because of an emergency. Two, you in good faith made a substantial beginning of performance before any cancellation notice. Three, and this is the one to memorize, the buyer gave you a separate, dated, signed personal statement, in the buyer's own handwriting, describing the emergency and expressly waiving the three day right.
Handwriting. Not typed. Not a checkbox on your form. Their own hand, their own words. Michigan requires it and the federal cooling off rule requires it too.

That means on a burst pipe or a tree through the roof, you get that handwritten waiver before you set a single fan, or you are working at your own risk with a customer who can walk for three business days.

If the buyer does cancel in time, you return every payment, any trade in, and any signed note within ten business days of receiving the notice. Business days, not calendar days. The buyer makes any delivered goods available at the house, and if you do not pick them up within twenty days, the buyer keeps them for free.
Question. Water loss at nine at night, homeowner wants you starting immediately. What do you need from them, in what form, and by when.

A separate, dated, signed statement in their own handwriting describing the emergency and waiving the three day right, before you begin, along with their request for immediate service and your good faith substantial beginning of performance.
Idea seven. Contract fundamentals, because PSI tests the national material too.

A valid contract needs five elements. Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, and legality. Consideration means each side gives something of value. If a party lacks capacity, a minor for instance, the contract is voidable by that party. An illegal contract is simply void from the start.
Then know your contract types by one question, who eats the cost risk.
Fixed price, also called lump sum. You carry the risk. Overrun the budget and you eat it, beat the budget and you keep the savings.
Cost plus. The owner carries the risk, paying your actual costs plus a fee.
Time and materials. The owner again, paying hourly labor and materials, and it is used where scope is genuinely uncertain.
Unit price. Shared. You carry the unit cost risk, the owner carries the quantity risk.

Change orders get written and signed by both parties, describing the scope change and the price or time adjustment. And in Michigan that is not merely good practice. Remember law one from the top of this chapter, written amendments are a condition of your lien rights.

Two completions to keep apart. Substantial completion means the owner can use the work for its intended purpose. It triggers release of retainage, which is typically five to ten percent held back from progress payments, and it starts the warranty clock. Final completion means every punch list item is finished.

On breach, a material breach excuses the other party's performance. Remedies include compensatory damages, rescission, quantum meruit for the value of work performed, and rarely specific performance, meaning a court order to actually do the job. And the injured party always has a duty to mitigate, which means you cannot sit back and run up damages you could reasonably have avoided.
Idea eight. The clocks, and the difference between a limitation and a repose.
Breach of contract in Michigan is six years, under M C L six hundred point fifty eight oh seven, subsection nine.
Negligence causing injury to a person or property is three years, under M C L six hundred point fifty eight oh five, subsection two.

Then the big one, the statute of repose, M C L six hundred point fifty eight thirty nine. For claims arising from a defective or unsafe improvement to real property, against a contractor, architect, or engineer, the action must be brought within six years from occupancy, use, or acceptance of the completed improvement.

Read that again. From occupancy. Not from discovery. A defect found in year seven is barred even if nobody on earth could have discovered it earlier. That is the entire point of a repose, it protects builders from claims that surface forever.

There is one exception, gross negligence. Then the claimant gets one year after the defect is discovered or should have been discovered, but never more than ten years after occupancy. So the ten year number is only the ceiling on the gross negligence exception. It is not the general rule, and an answer choice that offers ten years as the ordinary period is wrong.
Here is the one line version of the distinction. A limitation runs from the breach or the injury. A repose runs from a fixed event and kills the claim regardless of discovery.
Question. A homeowner discovers a hidden structural defect seven years after moving in. Ordinary negligence by the builder. What is the outcome.
Barred. Six years from occupancy under the statute of repose, and discovery does not extend it. Only gross negligence opens the extra year, capped at ten years from occupancy.
Idea nine. Warranties, in three layers.
Express warranties are the written promises in your contract, and they are enforceable exactly as written, no more and no less.

The implied warranty of habitability says a new home sold by a builder vendor must be fit for human habitation. Michigan recognizes it, but Michigan courts may enforce a disclaimer of it, so it is not untouchable.

The implied warranty of workmanship says the work must meet the standard of a reasonably skilled tradesperson, and it exists whether or not your contract mentions it. You cannot get out of it by silence.

Here is the classic scenario they build a question from. Bad flashing leaks three years in, and your one year express warranty expired long ago. What is the homeowner's best theory. The implied warranty of workmanship. Still alive, and still inside the six year windows.
Last, the insurance and liability round out.
Commercial general liability covers third party bodily injury, third party property damage, and personal and advertising injury. Never your own work product, and never your own property.
Builders risk covers the structure while it is being built, plus materials on site and in transit, and it ends at occupancy.
Errors and omissions covers design mistakes, which C G L excludes. If a question involves a bad detail on a drawing rather than bad installation, that is E and O.
Umbrella coverage adds limits and may broaden coverage. Excess only adds limits. That is the whole difference and it is a fair exam question.

A certificate of insurance is a snapshot. It proves coverage existed on the day it was issued and nothing more, which is why you re collect them. An additional insured endorsement puts the general contractor on the sub's policy. A waiver of subrogation stops an insurer from chasing the named party after it pays a claim.

And the liability theories. Negligence needs four things, duty, breach, causation, and damages. Strict liability applies to defective products with no fault required. Vicarious liability means the general contractor can answer for a sub's actions on the site.
Rapid fire recap. Say these out loud with me.

HIFA trigger, cash price over three hundred dollars, on installment credit, existing homes only. HIFA rescission, five P M, next business day. HIFA type sizes, eight point body, ten point bold headings. HIFA copy rule, no completed copy, no duty to pay. HIFA penalty, misdemeanor, ninety days, five hundred dollars. Liquidated damages for cancellation in a HIFA contract, prohibited and void. Home solicitation cancellation, midnight of the third business day. Emergency waiver, separate, dated, signed, in the buyer's own handwriting. Refund after cancellation, ten business days. Goods pickup, twenty days or the buyer keeps them. Licensure exemption, under six hundred dollars, labor plus materials. Unlicensed builder, cannot sue to collect. Lien rights, written contract, license number, written change orders, any dollar amount. Contract statute of limitations, six years. Negligence, three years. Statute of repose, six years from occupancy, use, or acceptance. Gross negligence, one extra year after discovery, capped at ten. Retainage, five to ten percent, released at substantial completion. Five contract elements, offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, legality. Four negligence elements, duty, breach, causation, damages.

If those come out cold, you own all seven contract questions. And if only one thing from this chapter survives the week, make it this, five P M next business day is HIFA financing, midnight of the third business day is the kitchen table sale. Keep driving.
